title: Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM)
summary: Toolpath generation, CNC programming, G-code fundamentals, post-processing, and machine simulation.

keyFormulas.label: MRR (Milling)
keyFormulas.math: MRR = a_p \times a_e \times f_z \times z \times N

sections.heading: What Is CAM?
sections.content: **Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM)** converts CAD geometry into machine instructions. CAM software generates **toolpaths** — the exact trajectories a cutting tool must follow — then converts them into **G-code** that a CNC machine executes. CAM sits between [[cad-computer-aided-design|CAD]] (the model) and [[machining-fundamentals|machining]] (the physical process).

sections.heading: The CAD-to-CAM Workflow
sections.content:
1. **Import geometry** — STEP or native CAD model into CAM
2. **Define stock & work coordinate system (WCS)** — the raw material and part zero
3. **Select operations** — facing, pocketing, contouring, drilling
4. **Choose tooling** — end mills, drills, inserts, with speeds and feeds
5. **Generate toolpaths** — the software computes cutter motion
6. **Simulate & verify** — detect gouges and collisions virtually
7. **Post-process** — translate generic toolpaths into machine-specific G-code
8. **Transfer to machine** — via USB, network, or DNC

The WCS must exactly match how the part is fixtured on the machine — a common source of crashed parts.

sections.heading: Toolpath Strategies
sections.content:
| Operation | Strategy | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **2.5D** | Pocket, contour, drill cycles | Flat features at fixed Z levels — majority of machining |
| **3D** | Surface finishing, Z-level, parallel | Sculpted surfaces, molds, dies |
| **High-Speed (HSM)** | Trochoidal, adaptive clearing | Constant tool engagement for faster roughing |
| **Turning** | Rough, finish, grooving, threading | Lathe operations |
| **Multi-axis** | 3+2 positioning, full 5-axis | Undercuts, impellers, complex aerospace parts |

Effective CAM is about **strategy choice first, parameters second**: a good strategy with moderate parameters usually beats a poor strategy with optimal feeds and speeds.

sections.heading: G-Code Fundamentals
sections.content:
G-code (ISO 6983) is the universal machine instruction language:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `G00` | Rapid positioning (no cutting) |
| `G01` | Linear interpolation (cutting feed) |
| `G02 / G03` | Circular interpolation CW / CCW |
| `G90 / G91` | Absolute / incremental positioning |
| `G54` | Work coordinate system selection |
| `M03 / M05` | Spindle on CW / spindle stop |
| `M06` | Tool change |
| `M08 / M09` | Coolant on / off |

A typical line: `N120 G01 X50.0 Y25.0 F200.0` — feed in a straight line to X=50, Y=25 at 200 mm/min. Feed rate is set by the CAM strategy and verified against the machine's capability.

sections.heading: Feeds, Speeds & Machining Time
sections.content:
CAM software computes the critical cutting parameters automatically:

$$F = f_z \times z \times N$$

$$T_c = \frac{L}{F}$$

$$MRR = a_p \times a_e \times f_z \times z \times N$$

where $f_z$ = feed per tooth (mm/tooth), $z$ = number of flutes, $N$ = spindle speed (RPM), $L$ = cutting length (mm), $a_p$ = axial depth of cut, $a_e$ = radial depth of cut. See the [[machining-fundamentals|Machining]] topic for the interactive cutting-calculator that computes these values live.

sections.heading: Post-Processors & Machine Kinematics
sections.content:
A **post-processor** translates generic toolpath data into the dialect of a specific machine controller (Fanuc, Siemens, Heidenhain, Haas). Different machines speak different G-code flavors, and multi-axis machines additionally need **kinematic transforms** — the post-processor must account for rotary-axis geometry to keep the tool tip accurate in five-axis work.

Post-processor errors cause real crashes. Always: simulate **after** post-processing, not before, and dry-run critical programs with single-block execution on the machine.

sections.heading: Simulation & Verification
sections.content:
Modern CAM includes full **machine simulation**: the virtual model of the actual machine, fixture, stock, and tool runs the posted program to catch:

- **Gouging** — tool cutting into the part geometry
- **Collisions** — tool holder or spindle hitting fixtures and clamps
- **Rapid-motion errors** — unexpected moves across the table
- **Excessive air cutting** — wasted cycle time

Verify before you run: the cost of a crash is measured in machine-hours and broken tooling, not minutes of simulation time.

sections.heading: Multi-Axis Machining
sections.content:
**3+2 (positional) machining** tilts the workpiece to five sides using a rotary table, then machines each face with standard 3-axis moves — ideal for prismatic parts. **Full 5-axis (simultaneous)** moves all five axes at once, enabling:

- One-setup machining of complex surfaces (impellers, turbine blades, molds)
- Shorter, stiffer tools (tilted away from interference)
- Better surface finish through constant tool engagement

5-axis costs more in machines, CAM software, and programming skill — justify it when multi-setup 3-axis work would accumulate tolerance error or when geometry is unreachable otherwise.

keyTakeaways: CAM converts CAD geometry into verified toolpaths, then into machine-specific G-code via a post-processor.
The Work Coordinate System in CAM must exactly match the physical fixture on the machine.
Feed rate F = fz × z × N and cutting time Tc = L/F govern cycle time and tool load.
Always simulate the posted program — gouging and collisions are expensive to discover on the machine.
Choose the toolpath strategy first; feeds and speeds are secondary tuning parameters.
